claimSlots.note: The guidance says nothing exclusive about who delivers exercise; it also describes self-management. The claim does not mention delivery.

claimSlots.statement: In the CSAW trial of people with subacromial shoulder pain, arthroscopic decompression gave no extra benefit over arthroscopy only, and the surgical groups' advantage over no treatment at 6 months was not clinically important.

claimSlots.note: Lancet; Elsevier user licence. Keep within the trial population.

scenarios.prompt: A client wants 20 minutes of activation before every session.
scenarios.goodAnswer: Keep a short warm-up (a few minutes); move strengthening into the main session with progressive load; no claim that activation fixes anything.

lesson.title: Correctives and activation: what the evidence supports
lesson.summary: What exercise research on shoulder pain actually compared, what it did not, and how to use activation drills as a warm-up rather than a fix.
objectives: Describe what research reports about exercise for subacromial shoulder pain, and for whom.
Explain why that clinical research is not a trainer's treatment plan.
Use activation drills as warm-up and rehearsal, without ranking them.
Know when a "corrective" should be a referral instead.

blocks.content: "Correctives" and "activation" are some of the most used words in shoulder training. This lesson separates what the research tested from what is coaching practice, so you can use both honestly.
What research reports, and for whom

For subacromial shoulder pain, a specific condition that a clinician diagnoses, UK specialist guidance reports evidence that exercise reduces pain in the short term (8 weeks to 6 months) and improves function. It also says that the most effective exercise approach remains uncertain.

In a large trial of people with subacromial shoulder pain, surgery to decompress the space gave no extra benefit over an arthroscopy without decompression, and neither surgery gave a clinically important benefit over no treatment.

For rotator cuff related shoulder pain, a 2020 systematic review compared each type of exercise with placebo or no treatment, not with each other. Progressive resisted exercise showed an uncertain clinical benefit, non-progressive exercise showed no significant benefit, and the certainty of the evidence was low.

content.label: Spindle policy
content.text: Your training is not treatment for a diagnosed condition. A client with diagnosed shoulder pain, or one recovering from surgery, a dislocation or a fracture, trains within the treating clinician's plan, and you do not progress that plan on your own. This is Spindle's rule for trainers, not a research finding.

blocks.content: Studies that record muscle activity (EMG) show that some exercises produce high activity in the serratus anterior and lower trapezius relative to the upper trapezius. Muscle activity during one session is not the same as gaining strength or changing symptoms.
Use that research to understand what an exercise asks of the shoulder blade muscles. It does not make any exercise the best one, and this lesson names none.

In a session, activation drills are rehearsal and warm-up: they get the client's attention on a position and raise the body's readiness to train. They are not a fix, and they do not need to take long.
Can the client hold the position you want under a light load, with smooth movement and no pain? Re-check the screen from lesson 4 the same way in a later session to see whether anything changed.

content: Position: set up the stance or support you will use in the first lift. Easier version: support the back against a wall or bench.
Light rotation: elbow at the side, turn the forearm out and back with a light band, 8 to 12 slow reps. Easier version: no band.
Shoulder blade control: reach the arms forward and let the shoulder blades travel around the ribs, then reach overhead along a wall. Easier version: reach only as high as is comfortable.
First pattern: the session's first press or pull with a light load, one to three cues only.

content.label: Stop and refer
content.text: Do not progress, and stop shoulder loading for the rest of the session, if pain comes on or rises with load, if the client cannot control the range, or if any warning sign appears. A warm-up drill that hurts is not a warm-up; skip it and refer if the pain is getting worse or has not improved after 2 weeks. A new inability to lift the arm themselves: urgent, today.

blocks.content: Give one to three cues per drill, as a direction or a target: "reach long through your hands", "push the band away". Watch the next rep, and keep a cue only if the movement changes the way you want.

content.label: Stop and refer
content.text: Correctives never replace referral. Any stop rule means stop for the session. Pain that is getting worse: routine referral now. Pain that has not improved after 2 weeks: routine referral. Anything in the urgent or emergency tiers: refer at that tier (see "When to refer out").

content.prompt: What does UK specialist guidance report about exercise for subacromial shoulder pain?
options: It reduces pain in the short term and improves function; the most effective approach is uncertain
One exercise programme is proven best
content.explanation: The guidance reports evidence that exercise reduces short-term pain and improves function, and says the most effective approach remains uncertain.

content.prompt: How did the 2020 review compare progressive and non-progressive exercise for rotator cuff related shoulder pain?
options: It found progressive exercise clearly better than non-progressive
It compared each with placebo or no treatment, not with each other, and the evidence was low certainty
It found no difference between them in a head-to-head comparison
content.explanation: Each approach was compared with placebo or no treatment; the review did not compare them head to head, and certainty was low.

content.prompt: An exercise shows high serratus anterior activity on EMG. What does that tell you on its own?
options: It builds more strength than other exercises
It asks a lot of that muscle in that session; it does not show strength gain
content.explanation: EMG shows muscle activity during the exercise. Activity in one session is not the same as strength gain or symptom change.

content.label: Talk it through
content.text: A client wants to spend 20 minutes on activation before every session. What do you keep as a short warm-up, and what moves into the main session as real training?
